topic: Why old railway tracks had gaps
script: Rail joints make a straight rail snake in summer heat. North America, 1890s. Talbot runs to a sudden buckle. Solid steel jerks a spike sideways. How do you stop rails from growing into snakes? The foreman rams two rail ends tight. Noon heat loads the rails; the track buckles. Talbot shows a tiny gap at the joint. Joint bars, called fishplates, have slotted holes. Heat a steel strip and clamp both ends; it bows. Leave a small end gap; it stays straight. Talbot and the team leave about one eighth to one quarter inch. Bolts guide the line while the ends can slide. Not for drainage, not to save metal. It is for heat that makes rails grow. A wheel hits the joint with a clear clack. Later, rails are welded and set to a neutral heat. The clack fades, but the rails stay straight. So the straight line stays straight.
